  2993	\label{sec:separablyClosedPoints}
  2994	
  2995	Over a separably closed field \(K\) the \(K\)-rational points of a smooth curve are
  2996	\emph{dense}: every nonempty open contains one. Over an imperfect separably closed field
  2997	not every closed point is rational (on \(\mathbb{A}^1_K\) there are closed points with residue
  2998	field \(K(a^{1/p})\)), so the algebraically-closed argument through closed points fails;
  2999	what survives is density, through the standard-smooth chart, which is \'etale over the
  3000	affine line. There is no classical source anchored here; the statements are as formalised.

  3002	\begin{lemma}[A separably closed field is infinite]
  3003	  \label{lem:sepClosed_infinite}
  3004	  \lean{AlgebraicGeometry.SeparablyClosed.instInfiniteOfIsSepClosed}
  3005	  \leanok
  3006	  A separably closed field is infinite.
  3007	\end{lemma}
  3008	\begin{proof}
  3009	  \leanok
  3010	  Suppose \(K\) had exactly \(n\) elements. The polynomial \(f = X^{n+1} - 1\) is separable
  3011	  over \(K\): in characteristic zero this is clear, and in characteristic \(p > 0\) the
  3012	  cardinality \(n\) is a power of \(p\), so \(n + 1 \equiv 1 \not\equiv 0 \pmod p\); hence
  3013	  the derivative \((n+1)X^{n}\) is a nonzero monomial, sharing no root with \(f\) (a common
  3014	  root would satisfy \(x = 0\) and \(x^{n+1} = 1\)). A separable polynomial over a separably
  3015	  closed field splits with distinct roots, so \(K\) contains \(n + 1\) distinct roots of
  3016	  \(f\) — more than \(n\) elements, a contradiction. (This mirrors the classical argument
  3017	  that an algebraically closed field is infinite, with the splitting input replaced by
  3018	  separable splitting.)
  3019	\end{proof}

1	\chapter{The \'etale plus construction of the relative Picard functor}
     2	\label{chap:PicardEtale}
     3	
     4	For a curve \(C\) over \(k\) and an affine test scheme \(\Spec A\), the \'etale-sheafified
     5	relative Picard group is computed by a single \emph{plus construction}: a class is represented
     6	by a relative Picard class on an \'etale cover of \(\Spec A\) satisfying a descent condition,
     7	and two representatives are identified when they agree on a common refinement. This chapter
     8	constructs that plus, on affine test schemes indexed by a \(k\)-algebra \(A\); we recall from
     9	elsewhere in this project the ambient functor it sheafifies. For an object \(T\) of
    10	\(\Over(\Spec k)\) write \(\mathrm{relPic}(C,T)\) for the relative Picard group of \(C\) at
    11	\(T\) --- the quotient of the Picard group of \(C \otimes T\) by the subgroup of classes pulled
    12	back from \(T\) along the second projection --- a commutative group, with restriction
    13	homomorphisms \(g^{*} \colon \mathrm{relPic}(C,T) \to \mathrm{relPic}(C,T')\) for a morphism
    14	\(g \colon T' \to T\) of \(\Over(\Spec k)\), satisfying \((\id_T)^{*} = \id\) and
    15	\((g \circ h)^{*} = h^{*} \circ g^{*}\). For a commutative \(k\)-algebra \(A\), write \(\Spec A\)
    16	also for the object of \(\Over(\Spec k)\) it determines via the structure morphism
    17	\(\Spec A \to \Spec k\) induced by the \(k\)-algebra structure of \(A\); a homomorphism of
    18	\(k\)-algebras \(A \to A'\) induces, via \(\Spec\), a morphism \(\Spec A' \to \Spec A\) of
    19	\(\Over(\Spec k)\). We abbreviate \(\mathrm{relPic}(C,A) := \mathrm{relPic}(C,\Spec A)\).

    23	The group \(\mathrm{relPic}(C,T)\) of the preamble is realised concretely as a quotient of
    24	the \v Cech Picard group of the product: this section records the quotient presentation and
    25	its exact coset relation, the calculus every later rigidification and degree statement
    26	cascades through.

    37	  from the base}: the range of \(\mathrm{pr}_2^{*} = \mathrm{snd}^{*} \colon \Pic(T) \to
    38	  \Pic(C \otimes T)\), so \(L \in H_T\) iff \(L = \mathrm{snd}^{*} N\) for some
    39	  \(N \in \Pic(T)\). The \emph{relative Picard group} is the quotient
    40	  \[

    42	  \]
    43	  a commutative group, with surjective projection \(\pi_T \colon \Pic(C \otimes T) \to
    44	  \mathrm{relPic}(C,T)\). The \emph{exact coset relation} holds: \(\pi_T L = \pi_T L'\) iff

297-On any ringed space $X$, the isomorphism classes of invertible sheaves
298-form a group; it is denoted by $\Pic(X)$, and called the (absolute) {\it
299-Picard group}.  Suppose $X$ is a ``projective variety''; in other words,
300-$X$ is an integral scheme that is projective over an algebraically
301-closed field $k$.  Then, as is proved in these notes, the group
302-$\Pic(X)$ underlies a natural $k$-scheme, which is a disjoint union of
303-quasi-projective schemes, and the operations of multiplying and of
304-inverting are given by $k$-maps.  This scheme is denoted by
305-$\IPic_{X/k}$, and called the {\it Picard scheme}.  It is reduced in
306-characteristic zero, but not always in positive characteristic.  When
307-$X$ varies in an algebraic family, correspondingly, $\IPic_{X/k}$ does
308-too.
309-
310-The Picard scheme was introduced in 1962 by Grothendieck. He sketched
311-his theory in two Bourbaki talks, nos.~232 and 236, which were reprinted
312-along with his commentaries in \cite{FGA}.  But Grothendieck advanced an
313-old subject, which was actively being developed by many others at the
314-time.  Nevertheless, Grothendieck's theory was revolutionary, both in
315-concept and in technique.
316-

318-review the history of the Picard scheme.  Reviewing this history serves
319-as well to introduce and to motivate Grothendieck's theory.
320-Furthermore, the history is rich and fascinating, and it is a
321-significant part of the history of algebraic geometry.
